title: Three Red Eyes, One Triage Desk

patient.name: Mdm Chua Ah Hoon
patient.presenting_complaint: Right eye has been red, watery, and sticky with discharge for the past 3 days, started after her grandson had 'pink eye'

history.hpc: Mdm Chua noticed her right eye became red and watery 3 days ago, with yellowish discharge that crusts her eyelashes together especially in the morning. She does not have significant pain — just mild irritation and a gritty feeling. She has no photophobia. Her vision feels normal. Her grandson, whom she babysits, had a similar red eye with discharge last week which has since resolved. She has not had fever or pain.
history.pmhx: Nil significant ocular history. Hypertension on medication.
history.social_hx: Lives with daughter's family including a young grandson. Works at a hawker stall.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: diffuse conjunctival hyperaemia, mucopurulent discharge with crusted lashes, normal-sized round reactive pupil, clear cornea. Left eye: mild conjunctival injection, no discharge.
examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed — not indicated for this presentation

investigations.va_distance: RE: LogMAR 0.1 (6/7.5). LE: LogMAR 0.0 (6/6). Vision is normal/near-normal in both eyes.
investigations.iop_nct: RE: 15 mmHg. LE: 14 mmHg. Both within normal range.
investigations.differential_assessment: Discharge MARKED, photophobia NONE, pain NONE/mild, VA normal, pupil normal and reactive — pattern consistent with conjunctivitis rather than iritis, acute glaucoma, or keratitis

diagnosis: Acute conjunctivitis, likely viral or bacterial, right eye greater than left, with probable household contact spread from grandson. Triage Category 4 — can be seen within 2 hours; not an emergency.

immediate: Apply the red eye differential systematically: ask about discharge, photophobia, pain severity, vision change, and pupil appearance
Note that discharge is marked, photophobia absent, pain absent/mild, VA normal, pupil normal — this pattern points away from iritis, acute glaucoma, and keratitis
Measure VA and IOP as part of routine workup — both are normal/expected
Document findings clearly on the SNEC Triage Form, including the household contact history
Assign Category 4 — conjunctivitis can be safely seen within 2 hours
Advise the patient on hygiene measures while she waits to reduce spread to others in the waiting area
follow_up: Doctor to confirm diagnosis and prescribe topical antibiotic drops if bacterial conjunctivitis suspected
Advise patient to return earlier if pain worsens, vision drops, or photophobia develops (would suggest a different diagnosis)
Document outcome of triage decision for case review/learning
patient_education: Explain that conjunctivitis is usually contagious and to avoid sharing towels/pillows with her grandson
Advise frequent handwashing and not rubbing the eyes
Reassure her this is a common, usually self-limiting condition that the doctor will manage
Advise her to come back sooner if she develops eye pain, blurred vision, or sensitivity to light

key_points: Asks about nature and amount of discharge (marked, mucopurulent, crusting)
Asks about pain severity and presence of photophobia (both absent/minimal)
Asks about contact history (grandson with similar symptoms) — relevant for infectious spread
Uses a structured approach covering the key red eye differential features
Measures VA in both eyes — confirms normal/near-normal vision
Performs NCT — confirms normal IOP, ruling out acute glaucoma
Observes pupil shape and reactivity — normal and reactive, ruling out iritis/AACG patterns
Applies the conjunctivitis/iritis/acute glaucoma/keratitis differential table correctly
Identifies marked discharge + no photophobia + no/mild pain + normal VA + normal pupil as conjunctivitis pattern
Recognises this is not an emergency despite the patient's concern about a 'red eye'
Documents findings and triage category accurately on the SNEC Triage Form
Provides hygiene advice appropriate for likely infectious conjunctivitis
Gives clear safety-netting advice (return if pain, photophobia, or vision changes develop)
Does not over- or under-triage the patient
